Sugar Land's city rate for Tax Year 2026 is $0.371116 per $100 of taxable value. That covers only the city share of your bill. The school district, Fort Bend County and any MUD or LID levy are added on top.

The rate has two parts: $0.220157 for maintenance and operations and $0.150959 for debt service, which repays borrowed money for city projects.

The city portion is roughly 21 percent of the residential bill in Fort Bend ISD and 19 percent in Lamar CISD, before any MUD or LID taxes. Your tax bill shows which district serves your house.

The city rate edged up in both Tax Year 2025 and Tax Year 2026.

For 2026 the no-new-revenue rate is $0.355381 and the voter-approval rate is $0.381586. The voter-approval rate is the ceiling the city cannot pass without a vote. The estimated annual city bill on the median homestead is $1,371 for 2026, up from $1,312 the year before.

Council votes on the rate in September, after budget approval and a public hearing. The city has 60 days after it receives the certified tax roll, or until September 30, whichever is later. Appraised values are certified by July 25, so the rate cannot be final until that roll is in.

Two reference rates frame the vote. The no-new-revenue rate raises the same money as the year before from existing property. The voter-approval rate is the most the city can set without an election, and it works out to debt service plus a 3.5 percent increase in maintenance and operations revenue.

The city's taxpayer impact statement shows a $4.90 monthly impact for the median homestead in 2026.

The city describes its rate as among the lowest in the state for cities its size. Since 1993 the rate has fallen from 50 cents to 35 cents per $100, which the city credits to economic development and sales tax growth. Over the same stretch the city homestead exemption rose from 1 percent to 15 percent.

Average home value in the city is $540,358 for Tax Year 2026, against $529,032 for 2025, with an average homestead exemption of $81,054. Those are averages. Your own appraisal notice and bill are the numbers to use when you price a house.

The city's homestead exemption is 15 percent of assessed value, plus $70,000 for owners over 65 and $70,000 for disabled persons. An owner who is both over 65 and disabled gets just one. A disabled veteran should contact the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District.

School districts have their own exemptions. The state-required school homestead exemption is $140,000, with another $60,000 for seniors and disabled owners. Older and disabled owners also get a school tax ceiling that generally holds the school bill at the level of the year they first qualified.

  • You must own the home and live in it as your main residence, with no second homestead claimed anywhere.
  • A buyer closing after New Year's Day can claim for the rest of that tax year if the seller never did.
  • Applications go to the appraisal district, not to the city.

The Fort Bend Central Appraisal District sets values. The Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector bills and collects under contract with the city. Send valuation and exemption questions to the appraisal district.

The appraisal district is at 2801 B F Terry Blvd, Rosenberg, TX 77471, phone 281-344-8623. Exemption applications need a copy of your Texas driver's license or DPS ID, and the address on it must match the property address.

Texas appraises property as of January 1. Notices for single-family homesteads go out around April 1, protests are generally due mid-May and the appraisal records are approved in July. A value you want to dispute has to be challenged inside that window.

Pay by January 31. A bill still open on February 1 is delinquent. If the bill was mailed after January 10, the cutoff moves to the first day of a later month that leaves at least 21 days. Seniors and disabled owners may split the bill into four installments.

  • Delinquency on February 1 adds a 6 percent penalty and 1 percent interest.
  • The penalty keeps climbing monthly until it hits 12 percent on July 1.
  • Interest has no cap, and a collection lawyer's fee of up to 20 percent can follow.

The tax lien stays on the land. It attaches on January 1, and whoever owned the house that day can still be sued for that year's tax after selling.

The closing agent therefore asks for a tax certificate and pays what is owed from seller funds. An unpaid account moves through notices, an optional installment plan and finally a suit, with costs added. A taxing unit can ultimately foreclose and auction the house.

If back taxes are why you want to sell, call the Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector for a payoff number before you price the house. With that figure you can compare an agent listing, a private deal and a cash offer fairly. Penalty and interest can sometimes be waived when the tax is paid soon after you learn of the delinquency, so raise that with the tax office. A cash sale skips lender approval, but the tax still gets paid at closing.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 city tax rate in Sugar Land?
faqs.a: $0.371116 per $100 of taxable value. School, county and any MUD or LID rates come on top.

faqs.q: Does Sugar Land give a homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Yes: 15 percent of assessed value, plus $70,000 for owners over 65 or $70,000 for disabled persons, one of the two at most. File with the Fort Bend Central Appraisal District.

faqs.q: Who gets my Sugar Land tax payment?
faqs.a: The Fort Bend County Tax Assessor-Collector, which collects for the city by contract. Value and exemption questions go to the appraisal district.

faqs.q: When does a Sugar Land bill go delinquent?
faqs.a: After January 31. February 1 adds a 6 percent penalty plus 1 percent interest.

faqs.q: Can I sell if I owe taxes on my Sugar Land house?
faqs.a: Yes. The closing agent pays the balance from your proceeds, so get a payoff figure from the county tax office first.
